conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. Thank you for making time today—caring for a new baby is demanding, and I appreciate you being here.

I’ll be guiding us through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, well-studied questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days so we can best support you in these early weeks of motherhood.

Everything you share is confidential and judgment-free; my only goal is to keep you safe and help you feel better. We’ll walk through 10 questions together. I’ll ask each one conversationally—no need to remember numbers or categories—and you can answer in your own words.

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.  
First, looking back over the past seven days, how much have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[offers a small, tired smile]  
Honestly, Doctor, I can still laugh—maybe not as easily as before the baby, but if my husband makes a silly joke or I see a funny reel, I’ll chuckle. It just feels a bit muted, like the joy doesn’t last long before I remember the next feeding or the diaper I still have to change.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes. I still laugh, especially when my little guy makes those funny faces or when my husband tries to swaddle the baby and ends up tangled in the blanket himself. But the laughter feels kind of… quick? Like it fades fast and I’m right back to worrying about whether he’s eating enough or if I’m doing everything “right.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some things—like taking the baby for his stroller walk or having my sister drop by for coffee—but it’s not the same eager feeling I used to have. Mostly I’m just relieved when something goes as planned, rather than actually excited. I guess my brain is always running through the next chore or possible “what-if” about the baby, so the enjoyment feels kind of watered down.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… sometimes I catch myself doing that. Like yesterday, he was fussy for an hour and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that bothered him through the milk, or that I wasn’t holding him “right.” I know logically babies just cry, but I still feel a twinge that it must’ve been my fault somehow. It’s not every hour or anything, just little moments when I’m already tired.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Mostly my worries are about the baby—like is he breathing okay, am I producing enough milk, will I mess up the vaccination schedule—but every so often I’ll feel this knot in my chest and realize I can’t even pin it on anything specific. It’s like an “all-over” sense that something bad could happen, even when the room is quiet and he’s peacefully napping. It passes, but it’s definitely there a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I haven’t had full panic attacks or anything, but a couple of times—usually when I’m alone with him at night—I’ll suddenly feel my heart racing and this wave of “what if I can’t handle this?” It’s like a quick surge of fear that I’ll do something wrong or that something awful is about to happen. It lasts maybe a minute, then fades once I take a few deep breaths or the baby stirs and brings me back to reality.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. It feels like the second I finish one thing—changing him, feeding, laundry—there’s already another bottle to wash or another diaper blow-out. I’ll be rocking him and think, “I can’t see how I’ll get through the next hour,” but somehow I do. It’s not constant desperation, more like being stuck on a treadmill that keeps speeding up when I’m already running low on energy.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m up all night crying or anything, but my mind does keep spinning once the lights are off. I replay every little thing—did I burp him long enough, did I fasten the car seat right—and by the time I settle, the baby’s already rustling for the next feed. So I’m getting maybe four or five broken hours; it’s more worry than actual sadness keeping me awake.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel down some stretches of the day—like late afternoon when I’m tired and the house is messy—but it’s not this heavy cloud all the time. It comes in waves, then lifts when the baby smiles or when my husband brings me a cup of tea. So yeah, I’ve had sad moments, but they’re sprinkled through the week, not every minute.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really. I got a little teary-eyed the other night when he wouldn’t settle and I felt like I’d tried everything, but actual crying—like sobbing—hasn’t happened since we came home from the hospital. Most of the time I just feel kind of flat or tired rather than weepy.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

No, never. I might feel overwhelmed or exhausted, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind. My biggest fear is not being able to care for him properly, so I want to stay healthy and present—I just need some help managing the worry and tiredness.

You've shared that the past week has felt like an emotional roller-coaster: you can still smile at your baby's funny faces, yet the joy seems to fade quickly as worries crowd in. You described waves of <sym>anxiety</sym> that appear without warning, brief surges of panic at night, and a persistent sense of being on a speeding treadmill. Although you're functioning and caring lovingly for your son, the pleasure in activities is <sym>dulled</sym>, sleep is fragmented by racing thoughts, and self-doubt creeps in when he fusses. You made it clear you have no thoughts of self-harm and simply want guidance to feel more like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 17, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient still finds some pleasure in activities but describes diminished enthusiasm and a qualitative change from pre-baby enjoyment, matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blame occurs "sometimes" and describes specific instances, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, diffuse anxiety that appears "a few times a day" without a clear trigger, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>"Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and difficulty coping, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly worry-driven insomnia with racing thoughts, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She reports frequent but not constant sadness that recurs in waves, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS score of 17 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Your responses show nearly daily <sym>low mood</sym> and <sym>loss of interest</sym> (<quote>enjoyment feels watered down</quote>), frequent <sym>anxiety</sym> (<quote>all-over sense something bad could happen</quote>), multiple <sym>panic spells</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, and <sym>insomnia</sym>-together meeting DSM-5 criteria for further evaluation. Item 10 = 0 removes immediate self-harm concern, yet the combined mood and anxiety burden warrants prompt assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to discuss mood and treatment options
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or therapist trained in CBT or interpersonal therapy for postpartum depression/anxiety
3. Consider medication consultation; many <med>antidepressants</med> are compatible with breastfeeding if desired
4. Plan daily 30-minute rest window-accept help from partner/friends so you can nap or relax
5. Practice 5-minute breathing or mindfulness whenever <sym>panic sensations</sym> arise; pair with grounding techniques like noticing five things you can see/hear/feel
6. Limit evening screen time; dim lights and use white-noise to improve <sym>sleep quality</sym>
7. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor change
8. Keep crisis numbers handy: Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773 or text 800-944-4773 (English/Español)
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: SCREENING NOTE – POSTPARTUM MOOD/ANXIETY (not diagnostic)

Symptoms/Concerns endorsed
- Dysmorphic mood: intermittent sadness, “flat,” joy “watered-down,” quick-fading laughter
- Anhedonia: reduced anticipatory enjoyment; relief rather than excitement
- Anxiety: persistent baby-focused worries, 2–3× daily free-floating tension, brief nocturnal surges of panic (“heart racing”)
- Guilt/self-blame: situational, transient (“something I ate,” “holding him wrong”)
- Overwhelm: treadmill sense, doubts about coping next hour
- Sleep disruption: difficulty settling related to intrusive worry; 4–5 hrs fragmented nightly
- No crying spells; no self-harm ideation

Pattern
Mood and anxiety symptoms cluster in late afternoon/night, improve with infant or partner interaction; functional impairment mild–moderate (sleep, confidence)

Screening significance
Meets sub-threshold mixed postpartum depression/anxiety picture; highest scores on anxiety items (Q4, Q5, Q6); low-moderate on mood items (Q8, Q9). No safety concerns voiced.

Risk factors noted
Primiparity, sleep deprivation, cognitive worry load, absence of self-harm intent

Plan
Continue monitoring with standardized tool (EPDS); reassess in 1–2 weeks or sooner if worsening mood, panic, or function decline. Education on sleep hygiene, support activation, crisis line provided.
